1.pericope_label: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, in the twelfth day of the month, the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, set thy face against Pharaoh king of Egypt
debates: What the date of the oracle is and how it is reckoned
Why the oracle stands after the prophecy against Tyre
What the charge against the king of Egypt is
outliers: Ellicott dates the word by the progress of the siege of Jerusalem and places it at a moment of fresh hope among the exiles, where Gill and Wesley reckon only from the year of the captivity and Gill lists four competing readings of the date
Clarke rests the charge of profanity on a report from an ancient historian that the king declared God himself could not dispossess him, a claim the others do not use
themes: A month answering to part of December and part of January
A relieving army that did not answer what was expected of it
A crocodile lying in the midst of its own rivers
A fisherman dragging out what he has hooked

3.pericope_label: Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river is mine own
debates: Whether the creature is a dragon or a crocodile
What the fish sticking to the scales figures
Where the wilderness of the threat lies
outliers: Clarke makes the fish the common people in insurrection against their king, where Wesley and Ellicott make them the people adhering to him and dragged down with him
Gill places the wilderness in the deserts of Lybia and Cyrene where Hophra fought Amasis, while Wesley names the deserts of Libya and Syene
themes: A crocodile basking on the sand-banks of its own river
A king who said not even a god could dispossess him
Insects burrowing under the scales of a fish
A reed that pierces the shoulder of the man leaning on it

8.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will bring a sword upon thee, and cut off man and beast out of thee. And the land of Egypt shall be desolate and waste
outliers: Ellicott holds that no period of forty years can be made out from history and that the literal fulfilment of the desolation was neither intended nor expected, against Clarke who identifies it with the reign of Amasis and Wesley who counts it from the thirtieth to the seventieth year of the captivity
Ellicott argues that the verse division is wrong, since the formula that they shall know that I am the Lord always closes a train of thought rather than opening one
themes: A river a king claimed to have made for himself
A land waste from one border to the other
A well the noon sun shone straight down into
A people passing into the condition of the wilderness

13.pericope_label: Yet thus saith the Lord God; At the end of forty years will I gather the Egyptians from the people whither they were scattered
debates: How the forty years are counted
Where the land of Pathros lies
What the baseness of the restored kingdom means
outliers: Clarke reports the view that Pathros is the Delta before setting it aside for Upper Egypt near the Thebaid, where Ellicott and Wesley take the southern reading without hesitation
Gill and Wesley both allow that Egypt was considerable under the Ptolemies, a qualification Clarke leaves out of his unbroken list of foreign masters
themes: A country named after the shape of a Greek letter
A city famous for its hundred gates
A kingdom kept low lest it recover its strength
A trust in Egypt that kept bringing old sins to mind

17.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the seven and twentieth year, in the first month, in the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus
debates: What the twenty-seventh year is reckoned from
Why the latest oracle stands in the middle of the book
Whether Tyre was actually taken, and what became of its wealth
outliers: Gill reports interpreters who take the twenty-seventh year to be of Nebuchadnezzar reign rather than of the captivity, where Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott and Henry all reckon from the captivity

Clarke has the Tyrians escape by sea with their wealth before the city fell, while Wesley has what was left preserved by articles of surrender, and Ellicott argues at length against the inference that the city was never taken
themes: A prophecy dated last and placed in the middle
Heads made bald by the constant wearing of helmets
A besieged city whose wealth sailed out of the harbour
A mole built from the mainland to an island

19.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and it shall be the wages for his army
debates: Who is paid with the spoil of Egypt
Whether Nebuchadnezzar conquered Egypt at all
outliers: Ellicott argues at length against the account the Egyptian priests gave to Herodotus, which makes the fall of Hophra a purely internal revolt with no foreign interference
Clarke, Wesley and Gill each name a different man for the budding horn, while Ellicott declines to name anyone and reads it of Israel reviving prosperity
themes: A king who spent blood and treasure and got nothing
Priests covering up what told against their country
A word spoken while the campaign was still under way
A horn spoken of as only in germ
